articles.summary: Wayne Mardle reflects on Luke Humphries' stunning comeback from 3-0 down to beat Gerywn Price in World Grand Prix final, what it could mean ahead of World Championship and why Price should not "beat himself up too much" after "disheartening" defeat
articles.body:
I may be wrong but, a few years ago, I don't think Luke would have hung in a game like that to win it.

That was sheer belief: guts and determination knowing that you can do it - and he can do it against anyone from any position.

When you have won before, and Luke has done many, many times and in many, many ways, there is that belief of, 'I'm under pressure but let's just see as I know if I settle down my game can win', rather than 'oh no, I am going to get beat or get embarrassed 6-0'.

He played his game and he won. I am not saying it's that simple but sometimes you have to simplify it.

When he won the fourth set he relaxed and Price tightened up.

Humphries was in trouble, then a bit more and then a bit more - so to get out of it was an incredible effort.

He was under the cosh for more than an hour but didn't succumb. He stood up to everything Gezzy threw at him, which was a lot.

Luke can now go into the World Championship thinking, 'someone stop me'. To do it in set-play registers and sticks with you.

If Humphries and Price meet in a World final, something could crop up. This is all about one-upmanship.

On to Price, and he says things in the spur of the moment but the way he competes, he wants it. You can't be as focused as he was in the final if you don't care.

It is disheartening and disappointing when you are 3-0 up and don't win but he has lost enough finals to know nothing is a given.

He is still a young man and will get many more opportunities. He knows he is good enough.

But let's get it right, the way Humphries played in the last two sets - a 106 average and a 107 average - is unplayable.

articles.title: Rams' third-down blitz pivot worked to perfection vs. Eagles
articles.summary: Rams defensive coordinator Chris Shula made a stark change in how he called the defense in the Week 4 win.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Rams completely changed how they defended third down against the Philadelphia Eagles in the team's 24-20 comeback win in Week 4. The results were striking, as the Eagles failed to convert on all 12 of their third-down attempts in the game.

But what was most interesting was how they thwarted Philadelphia. Los Angeles usually blitzes on about a third of their opponents' third downs. Against the Eagles, the Rams sent extra pressure on eight of Jalen Hurts' nine third-down dropbacks, an 89% blitz rate, according to The Score's Ben Wolby . It's one of the 10 biggest jumps in third-down blitz rate by any defense in the last decade, per Wolby's data, which covers every game since 2016.

The Rams held Philadelphia to just 172 total yards and 3.0 yards per play. They sacked Hurts four times and limited him to 12-of-27 passing.

The Eagles couldn't answer the pressure on third down, and they couldn't sustain drives because of it. That kept Los Angeles in the game until Kyren Williams' seven-yard touchdown run with 1:10 left delivered a 24-20 comeback win.

Credit to defensive coordinator Chris Shula, whose pivot worked to perfection. It was a clear change from the Rams' usual approach, and a defense that normally leaves its pass rush alone on third down turned the blitz into the difference against one of the league's top offenses.

articles.title: Tailgaters navigate new tailgating rules
articles.summary: New policies for tailgaters were put to the test Sunday as fans flocked to the South Philadelphia Sports Complex to cheer on the Eagles.
articles.body:
New policies for tailgaters were put to the test Sunday as fans flocked to the South Philadelphia Sports Complex to cheer on the Eagles.

Under the new policy , oversized vehicles can no longer choose their own parking locations and instead will be directed to assigned spaces in Lots D and N.

There's also a price increase for those oversized vehicles.

The updated pricing structure sets the cost at $200 for four spaces and $100 for two additional spots, with a maximum of six spaces.

"It was scary at first, but once you got in, they did a good job of moving people around," said Roosevelt Turner of Chester, Pennsylvania. "We got here about 9:30 p.m. last night. We have seven vehicles, two with trailers on it."

"It's not horrible, it's like, we would pay for extra spots if we were allowed to. I feel like it's very crammed and it's so many empty spaces," said Lauren Heron of Ambler, Pennsylvania.

"When you raise the prices, you're gonna have a lot of people who are not going to be able to do this. You know, it's not fair," said Lisa Davis of Cheltenham.

Louis Jordan with the Philadelphia Tailgating Association says it was a rocky start from the long unorganized lines to an early morning fight.

"We still have some things to work out. 100-percent. All in all, this is a lot better than what we thought it was going to be," said Jordan.

The Philadelphia Tailgating Association is set to meet with Sports Complex Parking Venture later this week to discuss what did and what didn't work and possibly make further changes.

articles.title: Joey Porter Sr. Breaks Silence on Son’s Trade to Cowboys: ‘We Dem Boyz!’
articles.summary: Former Pittsburgh Steelers outside linebacker Joey Porter Sr. broke his silence on his son Joey Porter Jr.‘s trade to the […]
articles.body:
Former Pittsburgh Steelers outside linebacker Joey Porter Sr. broke his silence on his son Joey Porter Jr. 's trade to the Dallas Cowboys. After a long, contentious contract negotiation, the Pittsburgh Steelers shipped Porter Jr. to Dallas late Wednesday night in exchange for a 2028 second-round pick and a 2027 sixth-rounder.

Porter Sr. shared a clip of him going to the Cowboys game on Sunday, sporting his son's No. 25 jersey.

"Heading to the game. How bout them, Cowboys! We dem boyz!" Porter said in a video posted on his Instagram.

Porter Sr. is a Steelers legend. He was inducted into the team's Hall of Honor last December. Seeing Porter Sr. in a Cowboys jersey and saying, "How bout them, Cowboys! We dem boyz!" certainly ruffled Steelers fans' feathers on social media.

The Cowboys defeated the Houston Texans, 34-30, on Sunday. Porter had a strong performance in his Cowboys' debut, too.

On 16 coverage snaps, Porter allowed 0 receptions for 0 yards on 0 targets, according to SumerSports .

The Steelers were expecting Porter to play on Thursday night against the Cleveland Browns, but after two days without an issue, Porter said his back flared up. He was ruled out for the game. That's when the Steelers had enough and traded Porter.

Porter revealed in his introductory press conference with the Cowboys that he felt disrespected during the negotiation process with the Steelers.

Porter, who's in the final year of his rookie deal, was seeking a new contract with the Steelers. But the two sides could not iron out a deal.

"Definitely, definitely. It was a hard process, a lot of ups and down. Definitely felt disrespected and undervalued," Porter said. "But that's old news now. That's how I look at it. I'm onto new beginnings and new chapters, that's how I'm looking at it."

Porter feels the Cowboys are showing him more value than the Steelers did.

"It was the value. I didn't feel like it was really that over there," Porter said. "[Dallas] is showing me that they value me more over here. That's really all I need to show what I can do."

According to Jon Machota of The Athletic, Porter and his entire family have always been Cowboys fans.

"My whole family been Dallas fans our whole lives. Even my dad was a Dallas fan, my mom and everything. So this ain't the first time we're gonna have stars in the house. But now that we're actually here, they're going to rep this pretty hard, so I'm excited about that," Porter said .

Porter Jr. had the receipts, too. He posted a photo of his dad and mom wearing Cowboys jerseys in 1995.

articles.title: Jaguars had five to survive in the secondary in 22-17 victory over Bengals
articles.summary: The Jacksonville Jaguars had only to five DBs against the Cincinnati Bengals on Oct. 4. Somehow, they survived an onslaught from Joe Burrow.
articles.body:
When the Jacksonville Jaguars went to a nickel defense in the final 23:48 of their game against the Cincinnati Bengals on Oct. 4, there was no one left on the sideline who could play in the secondary.

Antonio Johnson and Rayuan Lane were the safeties. Travis Hunter and Jarrian Jones were the outside cornerbacks. Jourdan Lewis was in the slot.

That was it. And the situation got nerve-wracking at the end when Bengals' quarterback Joe Burrow completed 10 of 14 passes for 126 yards on his last two possessions, including three in a row for 68 yards to take the ball from his own 17-yard line to a first down at the Jaguars ' 21 with 1:32 left in the game.

Jaguars vs. Bengals matches Trevor Lawrence, Joe Burrow. See photos

But exhausted physically and mentally, the Jaguars' secondary summoned the skill and courage to put a stop to Burrow's rally and preserve a 22-17 victory at the Bengals' Paycor Stadium.

The key was the final four plays when Jones covered one pass well to force an incompletion, broke up another and Lane tackled running back Chase Brown 1 yard shy of the first-down marker at the Jaguars' 11 to turn the ball over on fourth down and enable Trevor Lawrence to run out of the clock with two kneel-downs.

"It was a tough one, but we got the job done," Hunter said of the Jaguars (3-1) snapping a four-game losing streak against the Bengals (2-2).

"Whenever somebody goes, you have to be ready, next man up, with no jitters," Lane told Bucky Brooks on the Jaguars' post-game radio show. "We have a great locker room, guys who love each other, go out and play hard."

Jaguars had to put two CBs' on inactive list

The war of attrition in the Jaguars secondary started when starting cornerback Montaric Brown (hamstring) and backup corner Christian Braswell (knee) were ruled out for the game in the final injury report on Oct. 2. Rookie safety Jalen Huskey was a healthy scratch on the inactive list released 90 minutes before the game.

It got worse. Caleb Ransaw , who backs up Johnson at safety, hurt his knee in the first quarter and didn't return. And with 8:48 left in the third quarter, Lane and Murray collided trying to defend tight end Mike Gesicki on a 15-yard TD reception from Burrow, and Murray went to the ground.

Murray was taken in to be evaluated for a concussion and didn't return.

The Bengals had their own problems. Wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase , who had torched the Jaguars for 25 receptions for 314 yards in his previous two games against them, had three receptions for 27 yards before coming out in the second quarter after a legal hit by linebacker Ventrell Miller sent Chase to the concussion protocol.

Tee Higgins (11 receptions, 157 yards) and Chase Brown (11 for 71 yards) stepped in for Chase, and Meyers had seven receptions for 82 yards.

Jags secondary looked lost, tired until the end

Murray's loss left the Jags secondary with five survivors. They struggled when Burrow led the Bengals on a 79-yard drive and scored on a 1-yard plunge with 3:33 left (Burrow completed 7 of 7 passes for 64 yards) and then looked lost and confused as he went from his own 17 to the Jaguars' 21, with no timeouts left, in only three plays: Completions of 29 yards to Tinsley, 18 yards to Gesicki and 15 yards to Meyers.

There were 68 seconds left in the game and the Bengals fans were rocking.

Here's the sequence of the final four plays the Bengals ran from the Jaguars' 21-yard line:

First down: With Foye Oluokun and Josh Hines-Allen bearing down, Burrow tried to hit wide receiver Dohnte Meyers over the middle, but Jones broke it up.

Second down: Burrow had tight end Mike Gesicki open in the end zone but threw the ball short and into the ground. Travon Walker was close to pushing guard Dylan Fairchild into Burrow.

Third down: Burrow tried to find wide receiver Mitchell Tinsley on a corner route but Hines-Allen rushed Burrow hard and Jones was able to break up the pass.

Fourth down: Hunter was playing press coverage on Gesicki on the left and Lewis lined up opposite Meyers on the slot. Johnson and Lane were defending the middle of the field. Burrow had running back Chase Brown run a circle route on the right, past Olukun. With tight end Tanner Hudson staying in to chip Hines-Allen, Burrow had time to hit Brown in stride but Lane came barreling up and made the tackle with Brown 1 yard short of the first down.

Lane said there was no magic to the play. He simply let his instincts take over.

"It's football at the end of the day," he said on the postgame radio show. "I've been playing since I was 5, along with everyone else on this team … just go out there and let it fly."

Jaguars allowed most passing yards since 2024

The final numbers told just how busy the five DBs who finished the game were. Jones and Lane tied with Oluokun for the team lead with seven tackles (Lane's final stop was his sixth solo tackle), Lewis had five tackles and Hunter and Johnson had four each. Jones had three pass break-ups, Hunter two, Lane one and Lewis one, coming on his interception in the third quarter.

Burrow completed 39 of 54 passes for 428 yards, the most allowed through the air by the Jaguars defense since Jared Goff and Hendon Hooker combined for 449 yards on Nov. 17, 2024 in a 52-6 victory over the Jaguars.

But the Jaguars beat the Bengals for the first time since 2019, and the five-point final margin was the only number that counted.

articles.title: Why Joe Burrow's 'throw it more' mindset could be a problem for Bengals
articles.summary: Breaking down Joe Burrow's post-game comments about why he thinks the Bengals should be throwing the ball more
articles.body:
The Cincinnati Bengals have now lost two games in a row with the ball in their star quarterback's hands.

Joe Burrow , Bengals head coach Zac Taylor and Cincinnati's offense haven't been able to deliver at the moments they've needed it most, and because of that, Cincinnati has lost any head start it had in the division when it began the season 2-0.

It's still early, and no one should be panicking .

Photos: Bengals vs. Jaguars on Sunday October 4

But the fact that an offense with an elite quarterback, two of the NFL's best wide receivers and an offensive-minded head coach haven't won either game when they had their chances, poses a cause for concern. That includes the Oct. 4 loss to Jacksonville 22-17 at Paycor Stadium.

"You've got to execute in those moments," Burrow said. "Each play is its own story. You've got to try your best to execute as well as you can in the context of that story."

The Bengals returned all 11 starters on offense this season, the same offensive coordinator and head coach. Because of that, there was going to be no room for excuses on offense.

Through four games, the Bengals rank 14th in points (24.3), 31st in rushing offense (74.3 yards per game) and fourth in passing yards per game (277.5).

One of the areas the Bengals hoped to be better in this season was the run game. Cincinnati rushed for 23 yards against the Jaguars .

"We weren't good in the run game today; 23 yards was a reflection of how our run game was today," running back Chase Brown said.

To put the Bengals' run game woes in perspective, in the Bengals' most recent two losses, they've combined for 106 yards on the ground. Jacksonville rushed for 111 yards in their win over the Bengals in Week 4.

Burrow attempted 54 passes against Jacksonville, and the Bengals were still held to just 17 points. It begs the question: Are the Bengals becoming too dependent on Burrow throwing the ball and do they need a more balanced attack?

Not according to Burrow. But statistics suggest otherwise. The Bengals are 1-5 when Burrow attempts 50 or more passes.

Burrow said he thinks the Bengals should be throwing the ball even more. Here's why.

"Because I know we're great at it. Because I know that's what I do best and we're pass-protecting really well right now," he said. "Obviously, we'd like to get more out of the run game, but I know we'll make it work."The Bengals return their explosive running back in Brown who's begging for a monster year as he's in the final year of his rookie contract and wants to earn a second contract.

They return all of the same offensive linemen and the same run-game coordinators. So, why can't the Bengals run the ball more effectively?

No one will say. And Taylor refuses to call run plays for the sake of it. He believes the best chance for his team to win is with the ball in Burrow's hands more times than not.

And that's why when those instances occur, Burrow and Taylor must make the most of them or their way will be called into question.

The hope within the Bengals' locker room is that improvement is coming soon in the run game. Brown said they are "close" to hitting some big runs.

Cincinnati started off particularly slowly in this area last season. The Bengals didn't rush for more than 100 yards in their first six games of the 2025 season.

Taylor and his staff made a valiant effort to change things as the season went in hopes they could find more in the run game and had some success in doing so.

The Bengals rushed for 100 yards in their last four games of the 2025 season and nine of their last 11. They showed it can be done with these players.

There's reason to believe it can be done this season. But time is ticking, and as Burrow said, they need to find more "ways to score more points."

articles.title: Meet the 15 Epson Tour players who earned LPGA cards for 2027
articles.summary: Reagan Zibilski surged to earn LPGA status as 15 players secured their cards at the Epson Tour Championship.
articles.body:
Before the start of the Epson Tour Championship, nine players had already wrapped up LPGA status for 2027. But for many of them, the question remained – what kind of status?

The top-15 players in the Race for the Card standings at season's end earned status for next year, but there's a significant difference between those who finished in the top 10 and those ranked 11-15 in terms of number of LPGA starts.

Those who finished in the top 10 earned Category 9 status on the LPGA priority list, while those finishing 11th-15th earn Category 16. Among the categories listed in between Nos. 9 and 16 are: members finishing Nos. 81-100 on the previous season points list; the current season reshuffle; and the top 25 from Q-Series.

In other words, those who finished outside the top 10 will likely want to go to Q-Series anyway to try and improve their status.

Haylee Harford Sanchez held the 15th spot coming into the last event but dropped to 16th after a rough 76 in the final round. Kate Smith-Stroh dropped three spots down to 17th after a T-59 at Indian Wells.

Here's a look at how things shook out this week in the California desert, with Epson Tour Championship winner Reagan Zibilski leap-frogging dozens of players with a career day:

The 20-year-old Malaysian turned pro last year at the Amundi Evian after winning the 2025 Annika Award as the nation's top collegiate player while at Florida State . She won twice on the Epson Tour this season and finished solo second, one stroke back, at the season finale.

Mexico's Olivares posted 12 top 10s in 19 starts, including a win at the Great Lakes Championship at the Highlands in June. Led the tour in birdies.

In 19 starts this season, Kaleiya has 10 top-10 finishes and one victory at the Island Resort Championship. At 24, the former Pepperdine grad and Oregon assistant coach is the elder sister of Kiara Romero and will join her sister on the tour next season.

Second-year Epson player notched her first victory at the Greater Toledo Classic. Added two more runner-up showings to cruise to her card. The Indiana native and Clemson grad will be a rookie on the LPGA.

The 2025 Augusta National Women's Amateur champion was a rookie on the Epson Tour this season and won her first title last month at the Guardian Championship. The Spaniard added four more top-5 finishes on the season to sail through to the LPGA.

Thai player was a rookie on the Epson Tour this season. Won the Thai LPGA Tour Order of Merit in 2024 and 2025, and the WPGA Tour of Australasia Order of Merit in 2025. The 22-year-old's victory at the 2026 Reliance Matrix Championship set the tour's 72-hole scoring record at at 26-under 262.

The 20-year-old from China posted four top-4 finishes this season to earn her way back to the LPGA. First earned her card at the 2023 Q-School at age 17.

Former USC player turned pro in 2024. Won her first Epson Tour title at the 2026 IOA Championship, making her the third Black winner on the developmental tour. Came into the season-ender eighth on the Race for the Card list and held strong with a T-5.

The 28-year-old didn't win this season but posted four top-3 finishes in 16 starts to finish ninth in the Race for the Card. Ranked second on tour in putting.

One week after the former Arkansas player teed it up in her first LPGA event at the Walmart NW Arkansas Championship and tied for 56th, Zibilski had the round of her life in the Tour Championship. The closing 62 secured LPGA status for 2027, moving up 27 spots in the Race for the Card standings to 10th.

Former Wake Forest grad joined the Epson Tour in 2025. Came into the Tour Championship 10th place in the Race for the Card standings but lost valuable ground when Zibilski went crazy low in the final round to vault up the list. Kuehn finished 11th in the card race.

Former Stanford star and the 2025 U.S. Women's Amateur champion finished 12th in the card standings after a T-18 in the desert. Ganne won in her seventh start on the Epson Tour and notched four top 10s in 11 starts.

Epson Tour rookie won her first title last June at the FireKeepers Casino Hotel Championship. Helped Northwestern to the program's first NCAA title. Finished 13th in the card race.

Former U.S. Women's Amateur champion took a share of 21st to hold on to the 14th spot in the Race for the Card standings. The 25-year-old Auburn grad earned her first Epson Tour victory early in the season at the Carlisle Arizona Women's Golf Classic.

The 29-year-old Wagner regains her LPGA card after another full season on the qualifying tour. A rookie on the Epson Tour in 2018, Wagner closed with a 65 at the Tour Championship to jump up one spot and into the top 15.

articles.title: Commanders vs. Giants odds: Opening lines for Week 5 matchup

articles.body:

articles.title: UNC's top wide receiver enjoys career day in loss to Notre Dame
articles.summary: Jordan Shipp led the Tar Heels with 109 receiving yards during Saturday's loss. UNC's junior wide receiver would rather have the win.
articles.body:
For the third straight football game, your North Carolina Tar Heels scored 25 points. Despite playing third-ranked Notre Dame close throughout Saturday's clash inside Kenan Stadium, UNC faltered late in a 37-26 loss.

North Carolina (2-2, 0-1 ACC) tallied a first-drive touchdown when quarterback Billy Edwards connected with tight end Shamar Easter on a 6-yard, play-action roll out to the right. Despite two interceptions, Edwards also tossed two more touchdowns, while linking up with WR1 Jordan Shipp for a career day.

Shipp caught seven passes for a career-high 109 yards. After the game, Shipp detailed the reasoning behind his big game, but highlighted how it didn't matter because of the Tar Heels' loss.

"Just trusting the scheme and trusting my coaches, doing what everybody told me to do," Shipp said. "All that stuff, the coverages that we've seen in practice, same stuff they (Notre Dame) ran in the game. It's nothing that I did special today, it was just my day to make some more plays to help my team get closer. But like I said, none of that stuff matters. We lost the game."

This is exactly the leadership voice any team wants in its locker room. Shipp could have easily bragged on his career day, but he focused on team wins being more important than individual achievements.

Shipp returning for 2026 gave UNC a massive boost for its offense, which fans had high hopes for with new offensive coordinator Bobby Petrino . If Shipp continues to produce like he did against the Fighting Irish (5-0), North Carolina will turn tough losses into clutch victories.

articles.title: Five field goals enough for Vikings to beat Dolphins
articles.summary: A big game from T.J. Hockenson helped the Vikings improve to 4-0. The Dolphins are 0-4.
articles.body:
The Vikings never reached the end zone today. To beat the Dolphins, they didn't need to.

Minnesota won 15-10 on the strength of five Will Reichard field goals.

The Vikings were without their best player, wide receiver Justin Jefferson, but they got a great game out of tight end T.J. Hockenson, who caught all 13 passes thrown to him, for 119 yards. On Hockenson's last catch, he purposely went to the ground just short of the goal line at the two-minute warning, which was smart clock management as the Dolphins were out of timeouts and the Vikings just had to kneel down to win it from there.

Vikings running back Aaron Jones carried a big workload, with 20 carries for 94 yards, and while quarterback Kyler Murray wasn't great, he was good enough on a day when the Vikings didn't need to score much.

It didn't help Murray that the Vikings lost the left side of their offensive line, as left guard Donovan Jackson (knee) and left tackle Christian Darrisaw (neck) both exited the game with injuries.

The bright spot for the Dolphins was running back Ollie Gordon, who had a 100-yard game in his first start in place of the injured De'Von Achane. But Gordon was just about the only player on the Dolphins' offense who got the job done today. Miami quarterback Malik Willis struggled to find open receivers, and the Vikings' pass rush didn't give him much time.

At 0-4, the Dolphins look like the worst team in the NFL. At 4-0, the Vikings look like one of the league's most pleasant surprises.

articles.title: Lincoln Riley discusses USC’s 25-21 victory over Washington
articles.summary: What did USC’s head coach have to say after the Trojans improved to 5-1 on the season?
articles.body:
On Saturday evening, the USC football team defeated Washington 25-21 at the Coliseum. With the victory, the Trojans improved to 5-1 on the season and 2-1 in Big Ten play.

Following the game, USC head coach Lincoln Riley spoke to the media. Here are some of the highlights of what he had to say:

"Hard fought win from the guys. I'm feeling excited about some of the steps we took and some of the clutch plays we made. Defensively, we just kept answering the bell all night.

"Obviously, lots to clean up, lots to be excited about, and yeah, I'm proud of the team. I'm proud of the fight. We had to dig deep for this one, there's no question."

"Penalties were just massive in this game. It felt like for a long period of the game we were really outplaying them. But when you make some of those mistakes, you just kind of let them keep hanging around, and we just had missed opportunities that were penalty after penalty. So, we clearly have to do a way better job on that. We had alignment penalties, we had a couple dead ball personal fouls, at the worst times possible. So, despite all that, to overcome it and overcome what we've had to this week, and come out and get a win against a quality Big Ten opponent. We'll take it."

On the team's mindset when trailing 21-10 in the third quarter

"I mean, we were even pretty steady at half. We felt like we were outplaying them. We just couldn't get out of our own way a little bit, and that's going to be probably a defining thing for this team going forward, right? How much of that we can do. I am proud though that we never wavered. I felt like the guys didn't waver, the coaches didn't waver. We made the adjustments that we needed to. We didn't get into the poor us. We caused a penalty here, or should have this been called there? We just kind of had a whatever it's going to take attitude, and that's what it took."

"Our D line is the tip of the spear. We have put a massive emphasis in every way possible to make our D line as good as we can, and we're to the point where we need to expect a big time performance out of that group every week. They're good enough to do it. That's our mentality, and if they're going to be the tip of the spear, then they have to bring it every single week. And they did tonight. They largely affected the game against a guy that's challenging because if you rush him too much, you can open up lanes, and he can make you pay. But if you don't, then he can just sit back there. So I thought we did a pretty nice job finding the balance."

"I think this team has a real love for each other. They have a real desire to be great. They're not hard to coach. They came ready. I loved our mentality. Saturday, we had a heartbreaking loss in a game that we felt like we should have won, and we came back Sunday and they were energized and ready to go Sunday night. Really were throughout the week. So I believe a lot in this team. I believe a lot in the capability, and that just pushes me to want to do everything I can to get these guys ready to play to prepare them. Because, like I told you guys last week, win or lose, coming to sit here, I know we have a good team in there, and I just want to help these guys. I want to help these guys feel that."

"I think this team will take a lot of momentum into this next game. This will be a big game for us, a big opportunity, especially when you look ahead at some of the bye weeks and opportunities here. Looking ahead to get some guys back healthy. After those bye weeks you start looking at how many young players are making big contributions for us. You start to get excited about the trajectory of this team, and we knew if we could right the ship right here in this middle part of the season, that we'd give ourselves a good damn chance. So we did it tonight, and hopefully we can do it again."

articles.title: No, Jeremiyah Love's 'longest year' quote wasn't about hating time with Cardinals
articles.summary: Jeremiyah Love knows the Cardinals are a rebuilding team. He wasn't talking trash about them.
articles.body:
There's no need to sugarcoat it. Despite showing occasional feistiness, Mike LaFleur's rebuilding 1-3 Arizona Cardinals are, well, a rebuilding team. And rebuilding teams tend to be rather bad and occasionally very disappointing. That's to be expected. Even a Week 1 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers is not as impressive anymore, given what we know about how awful the Chargers really are.

But just because the Cardinals are struggling doesn't mean their young core players, like rookie first-round pick Jeremiyah Love, are upset. Turning into a relevant team is a process. It takes time. You can't lose indefinitely. Eventually, you have to show progress to prevent your players from breaking. But the Cardinals are nowhere near that point yet. Not even close.

That's why it's important to note what Love meant when he called the 2026 NFL season "the longest year" of his life after the Cardinals' 36-24 loss to the New York Giants on Sunday. He was not saying he was unhappy with the Cardinals or their current three-game losing streak. He was talking about managing a taxing workload with many touches on offense over an extended 17-game season for the first time in his life as an elite football player.

Love is the Cardinals' bell cow tailback who is getting used to those responsibilities at the highest level of football. Of course he would feel this way. It's understandable. To be clear, he wasn't even visibly upset about this dynamic, either! He was simply explaining himself and trying to give more insight into his personal experience as a star rookie.

We don't need to turn quotes into something they aren't. There is no controversy brewing over a talented young player being disgruntled in Arizona. At least not yet. That could always happen. For now, let the Cardinals rebuild in peace.

articles.title: Giants-Cardinals ‘Kudos and Wet Willies’: Deonte Banks the hero, Arvell Reese the star
articles.summary: Let’s hand out some praise, and some criticism, as the Giants take over first place.
articles.body:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The New York Giants are — somehow — 3-1 without quarterback Jaxson Dart and star edge defender Brian Burns. They lead the NFC East. Let's examine the game in our unique 'Kudos & Wet Willies' style.

Deonte Banks — In case you didn't know, this is what happened on the final play of the game with the Giants desperately trying to hold a 30-24 lead:

That is a Banks' game-saving house call four plays after being called for a phantom pass interference call that gave the Cardinals first-and-goal at the 4-yard line with :22 seconds left, seemingly dooming the Giants to a depressing loss.

"I thought you had to touch the guy for it to be pass interference," said head coach John Harbaugh of the penalty call.

No matter. The Cardinals never gained another yard. Three straight incompletions, including one on a pass breakup by Banks, set the stage for the final play. Banks undercut a slant intended for Cardinals' wide receiver Michael Wilson and took the ball to the house as a jubilant crowd at MetLife Stadium erupted.

Banks had four passes defensed in addition to his game-winning interception.

It's been an amazing turnaround for Banks, a 2023 first-round pick who had miserable seasons in 2024 and 2025 and not long ago seemed destined to be a backup cornerback and kickoff returner.

Arvell Reese — The No. 5 overall pick in the 2026 NFL Draft is getting better each game, and quickly turning into a star. Reese filled up the stat sheet on Sunday with nine tackles [one for loss], an interception, three passes defensed and a pressure that helped Greg Newsome get one of the Giants' three interceptions of Brissett.

Reese wasn't satisfied, saying he "left a lot of plays out there."

Reese said he wants to be a "game changer" and a "dominant player" but that he's "nowhere near" being the player he wants to be.

Maybe not, but after what we saw Sunday that is a scary thought. He's pretty darn good right now.

Malik Nabers — Nabers gave everyone a scare when he stayed down on the field briefly after a 39-yard reception in the first quarter. He popped up and ran off the field, though. Nabers finished with a big day, six receptions in seven targets for 112 yards (18.7 yards per catch), including that 39-yarder and a 25-yard touchdown catch.

This was easily Nabers' best game of the season, and the explosive plays bode well for a Giants' offense that desperately needs them.

Abdul Carter — The second-year edge defender told Big Blue View this week that he was "disgusted" by the team's pass rush productivity through three games. Sunday, he did something about it.

Carter did not have a sack, but he did make Cardinals' quarterback Jacoby Brissett feel his presence for the entire game.

Special teams (except for kickoff coverage) — There is so much to love about what the Giants did on special teams Sunday, and what they have done all season. Except for Sunday's kickoff coverage, which we will get to.

Rookie placekicker Dominic Zvada is now 9 of 9 after connecting on three field goals on Sunday. He his from 39, 50, and 52 yards — the last two being the longest kicks he has been asked to attempt thus far.

Tyrone Tracy had a 55-yard kickoff return that set up a Zvada field goal.

Punter Jordan Stout did not hit any 70-yard bombs on Sunday, but he did average 44.7 net yards and drop two of his three punts inside the 20-yard line. His best punt was a 47-yarder with the Giants clinging to a fourth-quarter lead that pinned Arizona at its own 3-yard line.

Charlie Jones replaced Braxton Berrios on kickoff return, and eventual on punt return after Berrios was ruled out with a foot injury. Jones contributed a 23-yard punt return that prevented the Giants from starting a fourth-quarter drive in the shadow of their own end zone.

Dennard Wilson — There are a couple of reasons to praise the Giants' defensive coordinator after Sunday's game.

First, even without Brian Burns Wilson found a way to finally get the Giants' pass rush cranked up. Check this nugget from NextGenStats:

The Giants blitzed on 53.8% of dropbacks in their victory over the Cardinals in Week 4, the highest blitz rate by a Giants defense since the start of last season. Jacoby Brissett completed 6 of 18 pass attempts for 55 yards, two touchdowns, and two interceptions against the Giants' blitzes while facing pressure on 52.4% of dropbacks (2 sacks). The Giants have called more blitzes with Brian Burns off the field, who suffered a season-ending injury in Week 3, blitzing on 47.1% of dropbacks with Burns off the field and just 23.7% with him on the field this season.

The Giants blitzed on 53.8% of dropbacks in their victory over the Cardinals in Week 4, the highest blitz rate by a Giants defense since the start of last season.

Jacoby Brissett completed 6 of 18 pass attempts for 55 yards, two touchdowns, and two interceptions against the Giants' blitzes while facing pressure on 52.4% of dropbacks (2 sacks). The Giants have called more blitzes with Brian Burns off the field, who suffered a season-ending injury in Week 3, blitzing on 47.1% of dropbacks with Burns off the field and just 23.7% with him on the field this season.

As noted above, Carter and Reese were fantastic. Tremaine Edmunds and C.J. Okoye has sacks — the first official sack of Okoye's career. They made Brissett uncomfortable, contributing to the three passes they intercepted.

More subtly, look at the run defense. After two drives, the Cardinals had a 14-3 lead and had run the ball — mostly to the edges of the Giants' defense — nine times for 81 yards (that's 9.0 yards per carry). For the remainder of the game, they ran 17 times for 42 yards, 2.5 yards per carry. I don't know what adjustment Wilson made, but whatever it was it worked. And it changed the trajectory of what looked like it might be an Arizona route.

Bryan Hudson — Hudson got his first start in place of John Michael Schmitz, and appeared to play well. There were no obvious breakdowns in the middle of the line. John Harbaugh said the switch isn't permanent, with Schmitz having missed time during the week for the birth of a child. Still, Hudson's play might give the Giants something to think about.

Kickoff coverage — The Giants allowed kickoff returns of 39 and 27 yards, uncharacteristic breakdowns for special teams coordinator Chris Horton's group.

Kayvon Thibodeaux — Getting the start with Burns out for the year, Thibodeaux was mostly non-existent. He had two assists on tackles. That's it.

Odell Beckham — Beckham created lot of good will during the summer as he worked to come back to the Giants after a year away from football. He made the team, but in the end the Giants cut him. In my view, Odell washed away all the good will he created with his social media tirade .

Jameis Winston — I think we probably just need to get used to the idea that Winston is going to be in this category every week.

There was, as is the way of the world with Winston, a lot of good and a lot of bad.

There were three touchdown passes. A couple of those came on brilliant plays. A 25-yard strike to Nabers. A play where he scrambled and got Malachi Fields open for a score. A tight-window TD to Theo Johnson.

There were two interceptions. One of those, created a six-point swing at the end of the first half, taking the Giants out of field goal range and giving the Cardinals a chance to add three points. The other one, on the first possession of the second half, was "allegedly" thrown to Darnell Mooney. It missed the receiver, though, by about 10 yards. That pick put the ball at the Giants' 37-yard line and set up a touchdown that put Arizona ahead, 24-19.

There were four sacks. I'm not sure what the tape will show, but I would venture an educated guess that Winston either could have avoided or actually caused all of them.

In the end, though, Winston has started two games for the Giants, they have won both, and they lead the NFC East.
